items.title: Concept: closures remember their variables
items.body:
A closure is a function that keeps access to the variables of the place it was created, even after that outer function has returned. The closures drills use this everywhere: a counter or flag that only the returned function can see, a cache that lives as long as the wrapper, a list of timestamps kept between calls.

Two things are worth keeping in mind while you read the closures solutions:

- Each returned function keeps its own variables between calls. For each wrapper, ask what it stores, and what value in that store means "not yet".
- The memory-leaks lesson explains when the garbage collector may free an object. Read its rule, then ask of each closure what it can still reach and for how long.

For each solution, name the variables the returned function closes over and what each one is for.

excerpts.quote: export function memoize(fn, keyFn = (...args) => JSON.stringify(args)) { const cache = new Map();
Closures are functions that remember variables from the place where they were created. These drills use closures for private state, memoization, event emitters, rate limiting, and small stores.

items.title: Claim the index before you await
items.body:
Each worker runs `const currentIndex = nextIndex; nextIndex += 1;` and only then awaits the task. Those two lines contain no `await`, so no other worker can run between them: the read and the increment happen as one step. When the worker then waits at `await`, other workers do run, and they find `nextIndex` already moved on. If the increment came after the `await`, two workers could both read the same `nextIndex` while the first was waiting, and **start the same task twice**.

Why the others are wrong:
- **incrementing after await would throw**: nothing throws; it would just run a task twice.
- **await captures a stale copy**: `await` does not copy variables; the risk is other workers reading the same value.
- **separate threads**: JavaScript runs these workers on one thread, taking turns at `await`.

excerpts.quote: while (nextIndex < tasks.length) { const currentIndex = nextIndex; nextIndex += 1; results[currentIndex] = await tasks[currentIndex]();

items.title: Reject the old promise, or its caller waits forever
items.body:
Each call to the debounced function returns a new promise whose `resolve` and `reject` live inside a timer callback. A newer call runs `clearTimeout(timer)`, so the old timer callback never runs, which means the old promise's `resolve` and `reject` would never be called. Anyone awaiting that promise would **hang forever**. So the newer call explicitly rejects the previous promise with "Debounced by a newer call", and the earlier caller gets a clear answer.

Why the others are wrong:
- **setTimeout allows one timer per closure**: there is no such limit; the old timer is cleared on purpose.
- **the old promise would get the new result**: each promise has its own resolve; it would simply never settle.
- **cancels the request inside fn**: `fn` never started for the old call, so there is nothing to cancel.

excerpts.quote: clearTimeout(timer); if (rejectPrevious) { rejectPrevious(new Error('Debounced by a newer call')); }

items.title: Write results by index to keep input order
items.body:
Several workers run tasks at once, and tasks finish whenever they finish. `results.push(...)` would add each result in the order tasks **completed**, so a slow first task would end up near the end, not at index 0. Each worker already knows which task it claimed (`currentIndex`), so writing `results[currentIndex] = ...` puts every result in the slot of its original task, whatever order they finish in.

Why the others are wrong:
- **push waits for a lock**: arrays have no locks; push would not slow anything.
- **double-counting**: each index is claimed by exactly one worker, so no task runs twice either way.
- **drops results of tasks that throw**: if a task throws, `concurrencyLimit` rejects; neither version records it.

excerpts.quote: const currentIndex = nextIndex; nextIndex += 1; results[currentIndex] = await tasks[currentIndex]();

items.title: A reachable closure keeps its data alive
items.body:
The garbage collector frees an object only when nothing reachable refers to it. The handler returned by `createLeakyHandler` mentions `bigData`, so the closure keeps a reference to it. The page registered the handler (for example as an event listener), so the handler is reachable for as long as the page runs, and so is the array it refers to. To free it, remove the listener or stop referring to the big data in the closure.

Why the others are wrong:
- **GC skips large objects**: there is no size exemption; the rule is reachability.
- **fill() arrays live outside the heap**: they are ordinary JS arrays on the heap.
- **console.log keeps everything**: the lesson attributes the leak to the closure.

excerpts.quote: let bigData = new Array(1000000).fill('x'); function createLeakyHandler() { return function handler() { console.log(bigData.length); // closure keeps bigData alive
The GC collects objects with no strong references from roots (globals, stack, etc.).

items.title: Concept: one thread, taking turns
items.body:
JavaScript runs your code on a single thread: it never runs two pieces of your code at the same instant. Async code still takes turns, and the lesson file `35-event-loop-and-concurrency.js` explains the rules for whose turn comes next.

Waiting work sits in queues. The lesson names two kinds, **microtasks** (promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`) and **macrotasks** (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O and UI events), and says where rendering fits. Read its "DEEPER BREAKDOWN" section and write down, in order, what runs after the current script ends: which queue first, how much of it, and when the page is painted.

Two habits for the quizzes:

- When reading async code, mark every `await` and ask what other code could run at that point, and what shared variables it could change.
- When a function keeps scheduling more work for itself, note which queue it uses, and work out from your notes what that means for everything else waiting, painting included.

items.title: Sync first, then microtasks, then the timer
items.body:
`console.log('1')` and `console.log('4')` are plain synchronous code, so they run first while the script is still executing. The promise callback is a **microtask**: it runs as soon as the script finishes. The `setTimeout` callback is a **macrotask**: it waits for the next turn of the event loop, after all microtasks. So the output is 1, 4, 3, 2, as the lesson file says.

Why the others are wrong:
- **4 ms clamping**: even with a 0 ms delay the timer is a macrotask; the order comes from the queues, not timing.
- **reverse order of scheduling**: there is no such rule; the two callbacks are in different queues.
- **higher thread priority, interrupting after 1**: nothing interrupts running code; 4 prints before 3.

excerpts.quote: console.log('1'); setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3')); console.log('4'); // Output: 1, 4, 3, 2
Microtasks (promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) run after current script but before rendering and next macrotask.

items.title: Tracing the sliding-window rate limiter
items.body:
The limiter keeps the times of allowed calls. On each call it first drops stamps that are at least `windowMs` old, then refuses if `maxCalls` stamps remain, and only stores a stamp when it allows a call.

- t=0: no stamps, allowed. Stamps [0]. **true**
- t=500: one stamp, allowed. Stamps [0, 500]. **true**
- t=900: nothing is 1000 ms old; two stamps remain, refused, and nothing is stored. **false**
- t=1000: 1000 - 0 >= 1000, so 0 is dropped; one stamp left, allowed. **true**

Why the others are wrong:
- **true, true, true, false**: stamps are only dropped when old enough, and 0 is not old at 900.
- **one call per 500 ms slice**: it is a sliding window of up to two calls, not fixed slices.
- **false at 1000**: the t=0 stamp has aged out, and the refused 900 call left no stamp.

excerpts.quote: while (timestamps.length > 0 && now - timestamps[0] >= windowMs) { timestamps.shift(); } if (timestamps.length >= maxCalls) { return false; } timestamps.push(now); return true;

items.title: Start here: lesson files, then practice drills
items.body:
This lab teaches JavaScript through numbered lesson files at the top level (`01-variables-and-values.js` onward, each with variants such as bug-hunt and think-predict) and a `practice/` folder of drills with tests.

The practice folder works the same way for every topic: read the topic's `README.md`, edit `starter.js` one function at a time, run the tests with `node practice/run-tests.js starter async` (with your topic's name), and only read `solution.js` after you have tried.

This pack draws mostly on:

1. `practice/core-js/closures/` and `practice/core-js/async/`: the drill READMEs and their `solution.js` files. Most questions ask why a solution is written the way it is.
2. `35-event-loop-and-concurrency.js`: the order in which sync code, promise callbacks and timers run.
3. `40-memory-leaks-and-gc.js`: how closures keep data alive.

Read each solution function slowly and ask what would break if one line were written the "obvious" way instead.

excerpts.quote: This folder turns the lesson notes into active drills with tests.
Read `solution.js` after you attempt the drills.

items.title: Clear the timer when the work wins
items.body:
`withTimeout` races the real work against a timer promise. If the work finishes first, `Promise.race` settles with its result, and later events cannot change that. But the `setTimeout` is still pending. Without `clearTimeout`, it fires later anyway and rejects a promise nobody needs, and in Node a pending timer **keeps the process alive** until it fires. The `.finally` clears it as soon as the race is decided.

Why the others are wrong:
- **race cancels the slower one**: `Promise.race` cancels nothing; the timer keeps running.
- **a later rejection overrides the result**: a promise settles once; the late rejection is ignored.
- **an unhandled rejection crash**: `Promise.race` attached handlers to the timer promise, so its rejection is handled.

excerpts.quote: timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(message)), ms); }); return Promise.race([promise, timeout]).finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));

items.title: A chain of microtasks never lets the page paint
items.body:
Splitting the work into chunks of 100 only helps if the browser gets a chance to do other things between chunks. `processChunk` reschedules itself with `queueMicrotask`, and microtasks all run to completion **before** the browser renders. Each chunk queues the next microtask, so the whole 10,000-item run happens without a single paint, and the UI freezes just as if it were one big loop. The file's own comment points at the fix: yield with `requestAnimationFrame` (or a timer) instead.

Why the others are wrong:
- **splice copying is the cost**: the problem is scheduling, not the copy.
- **a background thread**: microtasks run on the main thread.
- **waits for the next frame**: that describes `requestAnimationFrame`, not `queueMicrotask`.

excerpts.quote: function processChunk(items) { const chunk = items.splice(0, 100); // process chunk if (items.length) { queueMicrotask(() => processChunk(items)); // or better: rAF
run after current script but before rendering and next macrotask.

items.title: A JSON string as a cache key
items.body:
`memoize` uses `JSON.stringify(args)` as the key in a `Map`. That is convenient: two calls with arguments that look the same produce the same string and share a cache entry, even if they are different objects. The trade-off is that JSON is lossy. Values it cannot represent faithfully (functions, `undefined`, Dates and the like) can turn into the same string as something else, so genuinely different arguments may **collide** on one entry. The solution lets you pass your own `keyFn` when that matters.

Why the others are wrong:
- **only one entry**: each key is a separate `Map` entry; nothing is replaced.
- **primitives are skipped**: `args` is always an array, so it is always serialized.
- **objects always miss**: the key is a string, so equal-looking objects hit the same entry.

excerpts.quote: export function memoize(fn, keyFn = (...args) => JSON.stringify(args)) { const cache = new Map(); return function memoized(...args) { const key = keyFn(...args); if (cache.has(key)) { return cache.get(key);

items.title: Turn every outcome into a value first
items.body:
`Promise.all` rejects as soon as one of its inputs rejects. The clone avoids that by never giving it a rejected promise. Each input is wrapped with `.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)`. The second handler catches a rejection and **returns** a value, `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`, so the wrapped promise is fulfilled. `Promise.all` only ever sees fulfilled promises, so it never rejects and returns one status object per input.

Why the others are wrong:
- **try/catch with partial results**: there is no try/catch; every input produces a status object.
- **Promise.resolve swallows rejections**: it passes a rejected promise straight through; the `.then` handler is what converts it.
- **Promise.all ignores rejected promises**: it rejects for any rejection, thrown or not.

excerpts.quote: return Promise.all( promises.map((promise) => Promise.resolve(promise).then( (value) => ({ status: 'fulfilled', value }), (reason) => ({ status: 'rejected', reason }) )

items.title: A separate flag tells 'never ran' from 'returned undefined'
items.body:
`once` must remember whether `fn` has **run**, not what it returned. Many functions, such as an init routine, return `undefined`. With the shortcut `if (result !== undefined) return result`, such a function would look as if it had never run, and it would run again on every call, which defeats `once`. The `called` boolean records the fact of running, whatever the result.

Why the others are wrong:
- **caches per argument list**: neither version looks at arguments; `once` ignores later arguments.
- **caches a thrown error**: if `fn` throws, `result` is never assigned; the problem case is a real `undefined` result.
- **a pending promise equals undefined**: a promise is an object, never `undefined`.

excerpts.quote: let called = false; let result; return function runOnce(...args) { if (called) return result; called = true; result = fn.apply(this, args);

items.title: Start tasks inside a promise chain
items.body:
`runNext` increments `active` and then starts the task. If it called `item.task()` directly and the task threw synchronously, the error would escape `runNext` with `active` already counted, and the `.finally` that frees the slot would never be attached; the queue could jam. Written as `Promise.resolve().then(item.task)`, a synchronous throw inside `.then` becomes a **rejection**, which goes to `item.reject` for the caller, and `.finally` still decrements `active` and starts the next task.

Why the others are wrong:
- **retries once**: there is no retry anywhere in `createTaskQueue`.
- **parallel worker threads**: promises run on the same thread; nothing creates threads.
- **finish in enqueue order**: tasks start in order, but with concurrency they can finish in any order.

excerpts.quote: active += 1; Promise.resolve() .then(item.task) .then(item.resolve, item.reject) .finally(() => { active -= 1; runNext();
